doc.title: Jack Sheldon interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, February 15, 1999

title: How he improvises and keeps in shape
summary: Improvising on automatic pilot, practice, and keeping the trumpet lip in shape.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Are you a guy that, when you improvise, is it possible to describe in words what you’re trying to do or how you do it?

Well I’m trying to play those chords, and play interesting notes in the chords, and rhythm, and I have be really, a lot of it has to be on automatic pilot, because I can’t think of it. That’s why I have to practice so much, so that I get my body just kind of playing. And then I can almost listen to it myself, and things will happen. And I can direct it and everything. But a lot of it is on automatic pilot. And I compose, and I know what the chords are, and I know what notes I want to hit, and how melodies work out though, it will happen with my body and my fingers and everything. You know what I mean? Am I explaining it? You know what I mean.
Yeah. And you feel you have to be in pretty good physical shape to make that all happen.
Yeah. The better — it’s like a fighter really, you have to train like that. And the trumpet especially, you lose it so fast, your lip, it will just go away in a couple of days. Just like

you never played. It doesn’t seem right. And then there are some guys, they say Harry James didn’t practice that much. But he used to go to my teacher, Uan Rasey when he wanted to — he played duets with him to get back in shape to do stuff. So I mean everybody has to work on the trumpet hard.
